articles.text: San Francisco has just experienced the worst fire in its history. The loss foots up at least $2,000,000 and may go still higher. The insurance was very light, as the locality was considered a safe one.
articles.summary: San Francisco reported to have suffered the worst fire in its history, with losses of at least $2,000,000.

articles.text: The Minneapolis exposition was opened Monday and the machinery was put in motion by Mrs. Grover Cleveland pressing a telegraph key at Upper Saranac lake in New York state. Everything points to a complete success for the expositson.
articles.summary: The Minneapolis exposition opened Monday, its machinery started by Mrs. Grover Cleveland pressing a telegraph key at Upper Saranac lake.

articles.text: The commission appointed by the Secretary of the Interior to visit the different Indian reservations has received its instructions. In general, the mission will be to find ways and means to decrease the Indian reservations where it is clearly seen that they are larger than necessary.
articles.summary: A commission from the Secretary of the Interior is to find ways to reduce Indian reservations judged larger than necessary.

articles.text: On our second page will be found the portraits of the anarchists who were recently condemned to death in Chicago for murdering or inciting others to the murder of the policemen killed on the memorable 4th of May. No verdict has ever been rendered that gave more general satisfaction than the one which condemned these men to death. Their utterances consisted of the rankest kind of treason and all good men will look forward eagerly to the day when they shall expiate their crimes on the gallows.
articles.summary: Editorial approving the death sentences of the Chicago anarchists condemned for the May 4 police killings; their portraits appear on page 2.

articles.text: The hopes of our war-like citizens will be blasted by the news that there is now no chance of a war with Mexico. The Mexicans claim that editor Cutting circulated a libel against Mexican citizens on Mexican soil and for this was arrested and punished in Mexico; a proceeding recognized as legal by all justice and international law. Consul Brigham and Cutting affirm that the libel was only circulated in the United States. Even in this case the Mexicans claim that they would have the right to arrest and convict Cutting; a right which of course the United States will not recognize. Telegraphic reports indicate that Cutting was released yesterday.
articles.summary: Editorial on the Cutting affair, saying there is now no chance of war with Mexico and that Cutting was reportedly released.

articles.text: The motion made by Willis Eaton at the stock meeting, relative to the back taxes paid on account of Billings county is a good one and was unanimously carried. Between the time the railroad was built and the county organized many thousands of dollars were paid by the railroad to the Territory for taxes on that part of the road passing through Billings county. Subtracting the amount of expense we were to the Territory, there still remains a balance estimated at from $6,000 to $10.000. This amount is of course justly due to us and there seems to be no reasonable doubt that it cannot be secured. The Territorial Secretary's answer to a question relative to the matter that: "An unorganized county stands in the light of a garden to a gardener rather than that of a ward to a guardian," indicates that there may be some opposition to the measure, but its eminent justice stands a good chance of winning the required approval for it.
articles.summary: Editorial backing Willis Eaton's stock-meeting motion to recover $6,000 to $10,000 in railroad taxes paid to the Territory on account of Billings county before it was organized.

articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: The round-up camped at Sentinel Butte last night, having worked Andrew's creek yesterday. The OX outfit, which started the round-up, cut out about 600 beeves Tuesday and will probably ship to-day from Dickinson. All the river out-fits have been gathering beeves and the most of them will ship soon. The round-up will work up the river probably disbanding at the Neimmela ranch. The quality of the beef is scarcely as good as was expected.
articles.summary: The round-up camped at Sentinel Butte after working Andrew's creek; the OX outfit cut out about 600 beeves to ship from Dickinson.

articles.text: Clay Leighton, one of the men who stole some horses from the Morton farm near South Heart, two years ago, and after being arrested, escaped from the Dickinson jail, was rearrested at Buffalo Gap recently. Being brought back to Mandan, he was there sentenced to five years and eight months in the Bismarck penitintiory, where he is now "doing time" for the Territory. His partner Scott, who escaped from Dickinson at the same time, has not since been heard from.
articles.summary: Horse thief Clay Leighton, who escaped the Dickinson jail, was rearrested at Buffalo Gap and sentenced at Mandan to five years and eight months; his partner Scott is still at large.

The newly married couple have gone to housekeeping at the Cantonment and are nicely settled. They are both well liked and everyone will wish them a happy journey through life.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock and G. D. Kennedy were the sufferers by a runaway Monday afternoon, that might easily have resulted seriously. They were a few miles from town when the buck-board seat broke and in the confusion a line dropped. In attempting to recover it, the horses started to run and both passengers were thrown forward on the pole Kennedy falling under the wheels and Paddock "staying with the leather" on the tongue. An inventory of damages showed a sprained ankle and countless bruises on Kennedy while Paddock escaped with several scratches and cuts.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock and G. D. Kennedy were hurt in a buckboard runaway a few miles from town Monday afternoon.

articles.headline: Lightning's Deadly Work.
articles.text:
The sad news was brought in yesterday morning by Riley Brooks that George Fraser had been killed at eight in the morning by a stroke of lightning and that Ed. Connolly of the 13 outfit, was badly stunned at the same time. Coroner Martin and Moses Ryder started immediately for the scene of the accident and last evening brought in all that was mortal of poor George.

The particulars are about as follows: George and Connelly had started with a bunch of horses from the Ref. Car Co's. lower camp and had gone about five miles when the storm broke. Connelly, who suffered greatly from the shock, says that he scarcely remembers anything except that his horse jumped violently and that he became unconscious. When he came to himself, he looked around for George and saw him lying on his face some distance away. He went to him and after considerable difficulty turned him partly on his back, when he saw that he was dead. His clothes were burning, but Connelly, in his dazed and prostrated condition, found it impossible to put out the fire. He managed to ride into camp and tell the boys where the accident occurred, when he again became unconscious. Brooks started immediately for town to get assistance and a team went from camp to bring in George. It was found that the bolt of lightning had entered his head, bruising it badly. It had then passed through his body into the saddle, which it pierced full of holes, thence through the horse, which was instantly killed and into the ground.

Thus passed away one of the noblest boys that rode the range. Always pleasant, genial and kind-hearted, he was at all times and places a perfect gentleman; one of Nature's noblemen. No one was a greater favorite than he and his acquaintances became immediately his warm friends. We never heard an unfriendly remark about George while the good words spoken for him were legion.

His parents reside at River John, Nova Scotia, and were notified by Dan. McKenzie, who is also a native of the same place.

The funeral took place at two o'clock this afternoon, the services being conducted by Rev. Mr. Boylan of Glendive, who spoke feelingly of the lessons taught by the accident. The remains will be sent to his old home for burial. A fine metallic casket was ordered from Bismarck and in every way possible his friends tried to show their appreciation of poor George's worth.
articles.summary: Cowboy George Fraser was killed by lightning while moving horses from the Refrigerator Car Co.'s lower camp; Ed. Connolly of the 13 outfit was stunned; funeral held in Medora with Rev. Mr. Boylan of Glendive officiating.

articles.text: The total number of cattle received at the Chicago yards last week was 48,312, of which over 20,000 were range cattle. The market during the week fluctuated considarably, but Monday's prices were about the same as those of a week ago. The market altogether presents a more encouraging view than it has for some time. Shippers are bidding largely, a process that invariably raises the price. Montana and Dakota rangers are topping the market.
articles.summary: Chicago yards received 48,312 cattle last week, over 20,000 of them range cattle; Montana and Dakota rangers topping the market.

articles.text:
One of the greatest trials about a cow-ranch is to get the horse-herd "located," so that they will not wander away. When horses haye been raised on a certain range, they can be taken hundreds of miles away and unless watched closely, are liable at any time to return all those hundreds of miles to their native "stamping ground." Instances of this are constantly coming to light, but perhaps as remarkable a one as has ever occurred, happened in the case of a team belonging to John Manning, formerly sheriff of Lawrence county. As narrated by the Black Hills Pioneer, it is as follows:

When John Manning came from Montana to Deadwood he brought with him a span of small bay broncho mares. He drove them in a buggy for a number of years about Deadwood and then put them on his ranch for breeding purposes. They each raised colts for four years which ran on the range with them. A year or so ago the mothers left the range upon which they had been feeding with their progency so long, and returned to their favorite stamping grounds in Montana, many hundred miles distant, and from which they had been absent eight or nine years. Mr. Manning exhausted inquiry for the runaways and then gave them up as lost, thinking they had been stolen. Some time since he received a letter from a friend in Montana, saying his mares were back there on their old range.
articles.summary: Item from the Black Hills Pioneer about John Manning's broncho mares returning hundreds of miles to their old Montana range.

articles.headline: Fall Meeting L. M. R. Stockgrowers' Association.
articles.text:
The meeting was called to order last Saturday morning at 9:30 by Chairman Roosevelt.

Willis Eaton moved that the B—T brand be admitted to membership. Carried.

Moved by Willis Eaton that the fall round-up do not take place this year. Carried.

Chairman stated that outfits south of the railroad would work the country east of the Bad Lands.

Messrs. Tripp, Wadsworth, Howard Eaton, Brooks and Sewall were appointed a committee to confer with the chair after the meeting and arrange for round-up and line-riding east of the Bad Lands and north of the track.

J. L. Truscott was appointed a committee of one to represent the association at Bismarck, provided any legislation is needed by the cattle interests. He was authorized to use association money to the extent of $100 to pay necessary expenses.

On motion of Willis Eaton, our member of the Legislature will be asked to use every means in his power to obtain from the Territorial treasury the amount of back railroad taxes which have been paid in on account of Billings county.

The chair in giving notice that the next business in order was the election of officers, stated that he could not be here at the spring meeting and asked that his name be not proposed as chairman again.

After discussion in which the chairman again refused to serve, Willis Eaton nominated Henry S. Boice for chairman. Carried.

On motion of Howard Eaton, A. N. Jeffries was elected vice-chairman.

On motion of Willis Eaton J. L. Truscott was again elected secretary.

Meeting adjourned.
articles.summary: Minutes of the fall meeting of the Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association, chaired by Roosevelt, who declined re-election; Henry S. Boice elected chairman.

articles.text: Mingusville has been a little upset lately over a dispute in which justice may be meted out to innocent persons. It seems that a cowboy went from Mingusville to Glendive to get a check cashed. While in Glendive he was importuned by a gambler to join in a game of poker. The cow-puncher was altogether too "fly" to enter into any such transaction but the gambler still kept at him and finally followed him to Mingusville. At last the cowboy lost all patience and told the gambler to clear out. Even this hint had no effect and at last it ended in a disturbance on account of which the cowboy and two other good citizens have been arrested. From the facts as we learned them, it appears that the gambler will go free and the others be punished, a state of affairs we hope to see reversed.
articles.summary: A dispute between a cowboy and a Glendive gambler led to the arrest of the cowboy and two other citizens at Mingusville.

articles.text: Bob. Thompson has "skipped the country" and it is very probable that he will never again show up in the Bad Lands. Last Thursday he shot his revolver off in town and deputy-sheriff Ryder immediately swore out a warrant for him and after considerable difficulty owing to the fact that he would not walk, got him before Justice Copeland. Here he was fined $15 and costs which he paid. Soon after, mounting his horse, he rode up to where Ryder was standing and stated that he had come prepared to kill him, holding him up meantime with his six-shooter. After a parley, he put up his revolver and by a quick move, Ryder got it and turned the tables on Thompson. He was put in irons, awaiting the arrival of officers to take him to Mandan. Friday night he was allowed to sit unironed in front of Jorgens' drug store. While talking, he took his boots off and got up to "streeth his legs," which he did to such good purpose that he has not been seen since. It was a well-planned escape, as no one could expect a man in his stocking feet to get away in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Bob Thompson, fined for firing his revolver in town, held up deputy-sheriff Ryder, was disarmed and ironed, then escaped Friday night in his stocking feet.
